Newborn Care

Smith–Lemli–Opitz syndrome: diagnosis, inheritance and care

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Smith–Lemli–Opitz syndrome, or SLOS, is a rare inherited condition affecting how the body makes cholesterol. Its effects can range from subtle differences to serious health problems from birth. A diagnosis should help a family identify the person’s actual needs, rather than assume that every possible feature or outcome will occur.

What changes in SLOS?

DHCR7 gives instructions for an enzyme called 7-dehydrocholesterol reductase. This enzyme normally converts the sterol 7-dehydrocholesterol, or 7-DHC, into cholesterol. Reduced enzyme activity can lower cholesterol and allow precursor sterols and their breakdown products to accumulate. 7-DHC is a substance being measured, not the name of an enzyme test.

Cholesterol contributes to development before birth, cell membranes, nerve insulation and the production of certain hormones and bile acids. SLOS is not caused by a parent eating too little cholesterol, and it is not an ordinary high-cholesterol problem. Changing the diet cannot by itself remove the underlying genetic condition.

Growth, development and structural differences

Possible findings include slower growth before and after birth, a smaller head, a cleft palate, joined second and third toes, or extra fingers or toes. Learning and development vary widely; some people have substantial support needs, while others have mild findings and typical or near-typical development. A toe or facial feature alone cannot diagnose SLOS or predict learning.

Genital development can differ, particularly in people with 46,XY chromosomes: the urinary opening may be misplaced, testes may remain undescended, or external genital appearance may differ more substantially. These findings need respectful specialist assessment. Girls and people without obvious genital differences can also have SLOS and can be diagnosed; appearance does not determine who deserves testing.

Other features that may need assessment

Facial findings can include drooping eyelids, folds at the inner eye corners, eyelid creases, an upturned nose, a small jaw, and differences in the upper lip or ears. Unusual gums or teeth and eye problems such as cataracts can occur. These descriptions are clues for clinicians, not a checklist for judging a child’s appearance.

Other possible concerns include low muscle tone, seizures, heart differences, feeding problems, narrowing at the stomach outlet or bowel obstruction, and sensitivity to sunlight. Not everyone has each problem. Photosensitivity refers to skin reactions to light; it should not be assumed to explain every eye or behaviour symptom.

Autosomal recessive inheritance and family risk

SLOS usually involves disease-causing variants in both copies of DHCR7, typically one inherited from each parent. The two variants do not have to be identical. A person with one disease-causing copy is a carrier and usually does not have SLOS. It is not an X-linked condition, and having an altered copy from only one parent is not the usual explanation for being affected.

When both parents are confirmed carriers, each pregnancy has a 25% chance of an affected child, 50% of an unaffected carrier and 25% of an unaffected child who is not a carrier. These chances apply separately each time, regardless of sex. Shared ancestry can increase the chance of carrying a variant in the same gene, but family testing and counselling (not blame or a fixed count of ‘faulty genes’) clarify the actual situation.

How common is it, and why estimates differ?

Published newborn estimates often quote about 1 in 20,000–60,000, but frequency differs with the population and how cases are identified. Carrier studies have produced higher modelled expectations than some observed birth counts. A large 2017 study analysed mainly US carrier-screening results; it was not a count of newborns diagnosed with SLOS.

Pregnancy loss in severe disease and under-recognition of mild cases may contribute to the difference, along with study methods. Estimates derived by comparing groups do not predict one pregnancy’s outcome. Historical recognition has differed by ancestry and by the visibility of genital findings; neither ancestry nor being a girl rules out the condition.

Diagnosis needs the right laboratory tests

A clinical genetics or metabolic team combines the pattern of findings with specialised sterol testing and genetic testing. Elevated 7-DHC and/or disease-causing variants in both DHCR7 copies can establish the diagnosis in the appropriate context. A routine cholesterol result may look normal in an affected person and cannot reliably exclude SLOS.

The laboratory method, units and medicines matter: some medicines can raise 7-DHC without SLOS. Give the team the complete medicine list; do not stop prescribed treatment yourself. A variant of uncertain significance is not a confirmed diagnosis. If suspicion remains despite an incomplete result, the team may arrange further biochemical or genetic investigation.

Carrier and pregnancy testing

Once the family’s disease-causing variants are known, relatives can discuss targeted carrier testing. Cholesterol or 7-DHC levels alone cannot reliably distinguish carriers from non-carriers. Before another pregnancy, genetic counselling can explain the confirmed family risk and the available reproductive choices without directing a family towards one decision.

Prenatal diagnostic testing or preimplantation genetic testing may be possible in an at-risk family. A fetal ultrasound or maternal screening result can raise suspicion, but a normal scan does not exclude mild SLOS. A routine chromosome count or microarray does not replace appropriate DHCR7 or sterol testing. Ask what a result establishes and what it cannot predict about severity.

Start with an individual care plan

A paediatrician and genetics or metabolic specialist can coordinate growth, nutrition, development and relevant organ assessments. Depending on the findings, these may include heart and kidney checks, eye and hearing assessment, evaluation of palate, limbs and genital development, and feeding or bowel investigations. Not every person needs every test or intervention.

Feeding and swallowing support, tailored nutrition, physical or occupational therapy, communication and educational support can be as important as medicine. Selected operations may address a cleft palate, heart defect, limb function or another structural problem. Ask which problem a procedure addresses, what alternatives exist and what recovery support is needed; surgery does not cure the whole syndrome.

Cholesterol supplementation: a specialist plan

Cholesterol supplementation is commonly considered by specialist teams and may help some physical or biochemical problems, but evidence for the size and durability of benefit is limited. A small controlled study did not demonstrate rapid behavioural improvement; this does not prove that supplementation has no other health benefit. Developmental improvement is not guaranteed.

The preparation, amount, feeding route and monitoring are individual decisions. Food-based and prepared cholesterol products are not interchangeable; allergy and feeding safety matter. Do not copy a fixed egg-yolk count or add bile acids yourself. Bile-acid treatment may be considered for selected liver or nutritional problems, rather than automatically added for every person.

Why simvastatin needs separate caution

Simvastatin has been studied as an addition to cholesterol therapy to alter precursor sterols, not simply to lower an already low cholesterol result. A small trial in selected children reported biochemical and irritability changes. A 2022 Cochrane review found the overall evidence for clinical benefits very uncertain and no study evidence on survival or quality of life; possible harms remained important.

It is not a routine treatment to start or adjust at home. Liver and muscle injury and drug interactions are recognised statin risks, and a reassuring small trial cannot establish long-term safety for everyone with SLOS. If a specialist considers it, ask about the treatment goal, uncertain benefits, alternatives and monitoring. Do not apply a standard high-cholesterol dosing schedule to SLOS.

Follow-up, everyday support and the future

An individual plan should follow growth, safe feeding, bowel symptoms, development, sleep and behaviour, mobility, vision, hearing and any known organ or hormone problem. The team may monitor sterols and liver tests and review medicines that affect the pathway. Do not stop psychiatric or other prescribed medicines independently; ask the prescriber and metabolic team to coordinate decisions.

Discuss sun protection for photosensitivity, accessible learning and communication, family support and transition to adult services. New distress may reflect pain or illness, not simply the genetic diagnosis. Severe forms can be life-threatening, while milder presentations may be recognised later; a general syndrome description or one blood result cannot provide a certain lifespan or developmental forecast.

When a change needs prompt or emergency care

Seek prompt clinical advice for worsening intake, repeated vomiting, a swollen abdomen, difficulty passing stools, fewer wet nappies, jaundice, new eye concerns or an unexplained change in usual behaviour. Report new muscle pain or weakness during statin treatment. Follow any individual illness, feeding or adrenal-hormone emergency plan; do not force feeds or change doses yourself.

Get emergency help for breathing difficulty or pauses, blue/grey or unusually pale colour, a first suspected seizure, fainting or loss of consciousness, or a child who is floppy or difficult to wake. A baby under 3 months with temperature at least 38°C needs immediate emergency assessment. Do not drive yourself to emergency care; arrange another driver or an ambulance. Do not wait for a genetics appointment or for several warning signs together.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask the genetics or metabolic team what establishes the diagnosis, which family tests are useful and what the result cannot predict.

Get the feeding, cholesterol or other medicine plan in writing, including preparation, monitoring, illness instructions and who to contact; do not improvise doses or stop prescribed treatment.

Agree on current organ-care and developmental priorities, sun protection and follow-up. Share the emergency plan with caregivers and seek help for new symptoms rather than waiting for routine review.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organise appointments, prescribed medicines, feeding observations, laboratory questions and family priorities. It cannot diagnose SLOS, interpret a DHCR7 or sterol result, decide a safe supplement dose or predict development. Urgent symptoms take priority over recording information.

When to seek help

Use the individual feeding, medicine and illness plan. Breathing difficulty or pauses, blue/grey or unusually pale colour, a first suspected seizure, fainting or loss of consciousness, floppiness or difficulty waking need emergency help; a baby under 3 months with temperature at least 38°C needs immediate emergency assessment. Arrange another driver or ambulance rather than driving yourself. Seek prompt advice for worsening feeding, repeated vomiting, abdominal swelling, jaundice or new symptoms. Do not self-prescribe cholesterol, bile acids or a statin or stop prescribed medicines without advice.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • SLOS is a variable DHCR7-related sterol-synthesis condition; 7-DHC is a sterol, not an enzyme.
  • The usual inheritance is autosomal recessive, with family-specific counselling and testing.
  • Normal routine cholesterol or a normal fetal scan cannot reliably exclude SLOS.
  • Organ care, nutrition and developmental support should fit the person’s actual findings.
  • Cholesterol and simvastatin decisions require specialist goals and monitoring; neither is a proven cure.

Frequently asked questions

What causes SLOS?

Reduced activity of the DHCR7-encoded enzyme disrupts the conversion of 7-DHC to cholesterol. The usual genetic cause involves disease-causing variants in both copies of DHCR7, generally inherited one from each parent. It is not caused by an ordinary pregnancy diet.

Is it a sex-linked condition?

No. It is autosomal recessive. For two confirmed carrier parents, each pregnancy has 25% affected, 50% unaffected carrier and 25% unaffected non-carrier chances, regardless of sex. The two inherited variants need not be identical. A genetics professional should interpret the family’s results.

How is the diagnosis made?

Clinical findings are assessed with specialised sterol testing and/or appropriate DHCR7 testing. Normal routine cholesterol does not exclude it, and an uncertain genetic variant is not confirmation. Medicines and laboratory methods can affect interpretation, so use the specialist’s explanation rather than interpreting a result alone.

Can SLOS be treated?

Many specific problems can be treated or supported, although there is no single cure for the underlying condition. Care may include nutrition and feeding support, cholesterol treatment chosen by specialists, therapies, education and selected operations or organ treatment. The plan is individual.

Can a girl or a mildly affected person be diagnosed?

Yes. Obvious genital differences are not required. Some people have subtle physical features, and learning or growth needs vary. Absence of a stereotyped appearance or of severe problems does not settle the diagnosis.

Should I give egg yolks or simvastatin?

Do not start a regimen from a general article. A metabolic team should choose any cholesterol preparation and discuss whether other treatment is justified. No fixed egg count suits everyone, and simvastatin benefit and safety remain uncertain; it requires specialist assessment and monitoring.

Can testing help with another pregnancy?

Yes. Confirming the family’s variants helps carrier and recurrence counselling and may allow prenatal or preimplantation testing. Screening and ultrasound differ from diagnostic testing, and a genetic result cannot guarantee a particular level of severity. Discuss options before pregnancy where possible.

What should not wait for follow-up?

Breathing difficulty or pauses, blue/grey or unusually pale colour, a first suspected seizure, fainting or loss of consciousness, floppiness or difficulty waking need emergency help. Under 3 months, temperature at least 38°C needs immediate emergency assessment. Arrange another driver or ambulance. Worsening feeding, repeated vomiting, abdominal swelling, jaundice or new symptoms need prompt advice and the person’s illness plan.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
